claim: The nucleus accumbens (NAc) is important for learning from feedback.
source: The nucleus accumbens (NAc) is important for learning from feedback, and for biasing and invigorating behaviour in response to cues that predict motivationally relevant outcomes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general claim about NAc function.

claim: The nucleus accumbens (NAc) is important for biasing and invigorating behaviour in response to cues that predict motivationally relevant outcomes.
source: The nucleus accumbens (NAc) is important for learning from feedback, and for biasing and invigorating behaviour in response to cues that predict motivationally relevant outcomes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general claim about NAc function.

claim: NAc encodes outcome-related cue features such as the magnitude and identity of reward.
source: NAc encodes outcome-related cue features such as the magnitude and identity of reward.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about NAc encoding.

claim: Little is known about how features of cues themselves are encoded in the NAc.
source: However, little is known about how features of cues themselves are encoded.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Rats learned multiple sets of outcome-predictive cues in the decision making task.
source: We designed a decision making task where rats learned multiple sets of outcome-predictive cues, and recorded single-unit activity in the NAc during performance.
evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the study.

claim: Coding of cue identity occurred alongside coding of expected outcome in the NAc.
source: We found that coding of cue identity and location occurred alongside coding of expected outcome.
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data.

claim: Coding of cue location occurred alongside coding of expected outcome in the NAc.
source: We found that coding of cue identity and location occurred alongside coding of expected outcome.
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data.

claim: Coding of cue identity and location persisted during a delay period after the rat made a decision and was waiting for an outcome.
source: Furthermore, this coding persisted both during a delay period, after the rat made a decision and was waiting for an outcome, and after the outcome was revealed.
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data.

claim: Coding of cue identity and location persisted after the outcome was revealed.
source: Furthermore, this coding persisted both during a delay period, after the rat made a decision and was waiting for an outcome, and after the outcome was revealed.
evidence: This is a main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data.

claim: Encoding of cue features in the NAc may enable contextual modulation of on-going behaviour.
source: Encoding of cue features in the NAc may enable contextual modulation of on-going behaviour, and provide an eligibility trace of outcome-predictive stimuli for updating stimulus-outcome associations to inform future behaviour.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings stated in the abstract.

claim: Encoding of cue features in the NAc may provide an eligibility trace of outcome-predictive stimuli for updating stimulus-outcome associations to inform future behaviour.
source: Encoding of cue features in the NAc may enable contextual modulation of on-going behaviour, and provide an eligibility trace of outcome-predictive stimuli for updating stimulus-outcome associations to inform future behaviour.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings stated in the abstract.

claim: Some theories of NAc function emphasize a role in learning from reward prediction errors (RPEs).
source: Theories of nucleus accumbens (NAc) function generally agree that this brain structure contributes to motivated behaviour, with some emphasizing a role in learning from reward prediction errors (RPEs) (Averbeck and Costa, 2017; Joel et al., 2002; Khamassi and Humphries, 2012; Lee et al., 2012; Maia, 2009; Schultz, 2016; see also the addiction literature on effects of drug rewards; Carelli, 2010; Hyman et al., 2006; Kalivas and Volkow, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some theories of NAc function emphasize a role in the modulation of on-going behaviour through stimuli associated with motivationally relevant outcomes.
source: and others a role in the modulation of on-going behaviour through stimuli associated with motivationally relevant outcomes (invigorating, directing; Floresco, 2015; Nicola, 2010; Salamone and Correa, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NAc is tightly linked functionally and anatomically with dopamine.
source: These proposals echo similar ideas on the functions of the neuromodulator dopamine (Berridge, 2012; Maia, 2009; Salamone and Correa, 2012; Schultz, 2016), with which the NAc is tightly linked functionally as well as anatomically (Cheer et al., 2007; du Hoffmann and Nicola, 2014; Ikemoto, 2007; Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cues that predict motivationally relevant outcomes elicit conditioned responses such as sign-tracking and goal-tracking.
source: Task designs that associate such cues with rewarding outcomes provide a convenient access point, eliciting conditioned responses such as sign-tracking and goal-tracking (Hearst and Jenkins, 1974; Robinson and Flagel, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cues that predict motivationally relevant outcomes elicit Pavlovian-instrumental transfer.
source: Pavlovian-instrumental transfer (Estes, 1943; Rescorla and Solomon, 1967)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cues that predict motivationally relevant outcomes elicit enhanced response vigor.
source: and enhanced response vigor (Nicola, 2010; Niv et al., 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Conditioned responses to outcome-predictive cues tend to be affected by NAc manipulations.
source: which tend to be affected by NAc manipulations (Chang et al., 2012; Corbit and Balleine, 2011; Flagel et al., 2011; although not always straightforwardly; Chang and Holland, 2013; Giertler et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NAc responses transfer from outcome to the cue with learning.
source: Similarly, analysis of RPEs typically proceeds by establishing an association between a cue and subsequent reward, with NAc responses transferring from outcome to the cue with learning (Day et al., 2007; Roitman et al., 2005; Schultz et al., 1997; Setlow et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Substantial work has been done on the coding of outcomes predicted by cues in the NAc.
source: Surprisingly, although substantial work has been done on the coding of outcomes predicted by such cues (Atallah et al., 2014; Bissonette et al., 2013; Cooch et al., 2015; Cromwell and Schultz, 2003; Day et al., 2006; Goldstein et al., 2012; Hassani et al., 2001; Hollerman et al., 1998; Lansink et al., 2012; McGinty et al., 2013; Nicola et al., 2004; Roesch et al., 2009; Roitman et al., 2005; Saddoris et al., 2011; Setlow et al., 2003; Sugam et al., 2014; Schultz et al., 1992; West and Carelli, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Much less is known about how outcome-predictive cues themselves are encoded in the NAc.
source: much less is known about how outcome-predictive cues themselves are encoded in the NAc (but see; Sleezer et al., 2016).
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: In reinforcement learning, motivationally relevant outcomes are typically temporally delayed relative to the cues that predict them.
source: First, in reinforcement learning, motivationally relevant outcomes are typically temporally delayed relative to the cues that predict them.
evidence: This is a general principle of reinforcement learning.

claim: To solve the problem of assigning credit across temporal gaps, some trace of preceding activity needs to be maintained.
source: In order to solve the problem of assigning credit (or blame) across such temporal gaps, some trace of preceding activity needs to be maintained (Lee et al., 2012; Sutton and Barto, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to reinforcement learning literature.

claim: NAc is a primary target of dopamine signals interpretable as RPEs.
source: Since NAc is a primary target of dopamine signals interpretable as RPEs, and NAc lesions impair RPEs related to timing, its activity trace will help determine what can be learned when RPEs arrive (Hamid et al., 2016; Hart et al., 2014; Ikemoto, 2007; McDannald et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NAc lesions impair RPEs related to timing.
source: Since NAc is a primary target of dopamine signals interpretable as RPEs, and NAc lesions impair RPEs related to timing, its activity trace will help determine what can be learned when RPEs arrive (Hamid et al., 2016; Hart et al., 2014; Ikemoto, 2007; McDannald et al., 2011; Takahashi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NAc is thought to represent a domain-general subjective value signal for different offers in a neuroeconomic framework.
source: Similarly, in a neuroeconomic framework, NAc is thought to represent a domain-general subjective value signal for different offers (Peters and Büchel, 2009; Levy and Glimcher, 2012; Bartra et al., 2013; Sescousse et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to neuroeconomic literature.

claim: Having a representation of the offer itself alongside a value signal would provide a potential neural substrate for updating offer value.
source: having a representation of the offer itself alongside this value signal would provide a potential neural substrate for updating offer value.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the functional significance of representing offers.

claim: The relevance of cues typically depends on 'context' for on-going behaviour.
source: Second, for on-going behaviour, the relevance of cues typically depends on 'context'.
evidence: This is a general principle about cue processing.

claim: Context may include the identity of a preceding cue in experimental settings.
source: In experimental settings, context may include the identity of a preceding cue, spatial or configural arrangements (Bouton, 1993; Holland, 1992; Honey et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Context may include spatial or configural arrangements in experimental settings.
source: In experimental settings, context may include the identity of a preceding cue, spatial or configural arrangements (Bouton, 1993; Holland, 1992; Honey et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Context may include unsignaled rule changes in experimental settings.
source: and unsignaled rule changes, as occurs in set shifting and other cognitive control tasks (Cohen and Servan-Schreiber, 1992; Floresco et al., 2006; Grant and Berg, 1948; Sleezer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Representation of cue identity would allow for context-dependent mapping of outcomes predicted by specific cues.
source: Representation of cue identity would allow for context-dependent mapping of outcomes predicted by specific cues.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the functional significance of cue identity representation.

claim: Rats were trained to discriminate between cues signalling the availability and absence of reward on a square track with four identical arms.
source: Rats were trained to discriminate between cues signalling the availability and absence of reward on a square track with four identical arms for two distinct set of cues (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: During each session, rats were presented sequentially with two behavioural blocks containing cues from different sensory modalities, a light and a sound block.
source: During each session, rats were presented sequentially with two behavioural blocks containing cues from different sensory modalities, a light and a sound block, with each block containing a cue that signalled the availability of reward (reward-available), and a cue that signalled the absence of reward (reward-unavailable).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Each block contained a cue that signalled the availability of reward (reward-available), and a cue that signalled the absence of reward (reward-unavailable).
source: During each session, rats were presented sequentially with two behavioural blocks containing cues from different sensory modalities, a light and a sound block, with each block containing a cue that signalled the availability of reward (reward-available), and a cue that signalled the absence of reward (reward-unavailable).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: All four rats learned to discriminate between the reward-available and reward-unavailable cues for both the light and sound blocks.
source: All four rats learned to discriminate between the reward-available and reward-unavailable cues for both the light and sound blocks as determined by reaching significance (p < .05) on a daily chi-square test comparing approach behaviour for reward-available and reward-unavailable cues for each block, for at least three consecutive days (range for time to criterion: 22–57 days).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment.

claim: The likelihood of a rat to make an approach was influenced by whether a reward-available or reward-unavailable cue was presented.
source: Analyses revealed that the likelihood of a rat to make an approach was influenced by whether a reward-available or reward-unavailable cue was presented, but was not significantly modulated by whether the rat was presented with a light or sound cue (Percentage approached: light reward-available = 97%; light reward-unavailable = 34%; sound reward-available = 91%; sound reward-unavailable = 35%; cue identity p = .115; cue outcome p < .001; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The likelihood of a rat to make an approach was not significantly modulated by whether the rat was presented with a light or sound cue.
source: Analyses revealed that the likelihood of a rat to make an approach was influenced by whether a reward-available or reward-unavailable cue was presented, but was not significantly modulated by whether the rat was presented with a light or sound cue (Percentage approached: light reward-available = 97%; light reward-unavailable = 34%; sound reward-available = 91%; sound reward-unavailable = 35%; cue identity p = .115; cue outcome p < .001; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Adding block half into the model did not improve prediction of behavioural performance, arguing against within-session learning.
source: Additional analyses separated each block into two halves to assess possible within session learning. Adding block half into the model did not improve prediction of behavioural performance (p = .86), arguing against within-session learning.
evidence: This is a behavioral result from the experiment.

claim: Rats successfully discriminated the cues according to whether or not they signalled the availability of reward at the reward receptacle.
source: Thus, rats successfully discriminated the cues according to whether or not they signalled the availability of reward at the reward receptacle.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral results.

claim: A total of 443 units with > 200 spikes were recorded in the NAc from 4 rats over 57 sessions.
source: We recorded a total of 443 units with > 200 spikes in the NAc from 4 rats over 57 sessions (Table 1; range: 12 – 18 sessions per rat) while they performed a cue discrimination task (Figure 2A).
evidence: This describes the neural recording data collected.

claim: Units that exhibited a drift in firing rate over the course of either block were excluded from further analysis, leaving 344 units for further analysis.
source: Units that exhibited a drift in firing rate over the course of either block, as measured by a Mann-Whitney U test comparing firing rates for the first and second half of trials within a block, were excluded from further analysis, leaving 344 units for further analysis.
evidence: This describes the data analysis procedure.

claim: The activity of 133 (39%) of the 344 units were modulated by the cue.
source: The activity of 133 (39%) of these 344 units were modulated by the cue, as determined by comparing 1 s pre- and post-cue activity with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with more showing a decrease in firing (n = 103) than an increase (n = 30) around the time of cue-onset (Table 1).
evidence: This is a neural recording result from the experiment.

claim: More units showed a decrease in firing (n = 103) than an increase (n = 30) around the time of cue-onset.
source: The activity of 133 (39%) of these 344 units were modulated by the cue, as determined by comparing 1 s pre- and post-cue activity with a Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with more showing a decrease in firing (n = 103) than an increase (n = 30) around the time of cue-onset (Table 1).
evidence: This is a neural recording result from the experiment.

claim: Within the cue-modulated units, 24 were classified as putative fast spiking interneurons (FSIs), while 109 were classified as putative medium spiny neurons (MSNs).
source: Within this group, 24 were classified as putative fast spiking interneurons (FSIs), while 109 were classified as putative medium spiny neurons (MSNs).
evidence: This describes the classification of recorded units.

claim: Several patterns of firing activity were observed upon visual inspection, including units that discriminated firing upon cue-onset across various cue conditions.
source: Upon visual inspection, we observed several patterns of firing activity, including units that discriminated firing upon cue-onset across various cue conditions, showed sustained differences in firing across cue conditions, had transient responses to the cue, showed a ramping of activity starting at cue-onset, and showed elevated activity immediately preceding cue-onset (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes observed patterns in the neural data, illustrated in figures.

claim: A variety of task parameters accounted for a significant portion of firing rate variance in NAc cue-modulated units.
source: Fitting GLMs to all trials within a session revealed that a variety of task parameters accounted for a significant portion of firing rate variance in NAc cue-modulated units (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the GLM analysis, shown in figures and table.

claim: A significant proportion of units (~32% of cue-modulated units) discriminated between the light and sound block (identity coding), accounting for ~5% of firing rate variance.
source: Notably, a significant proportion of units discriminated between the light and sound block (identity coding: ~32% of cue-modulated units, accounting for ~5% of firing rate variance)
evidence: This is a result from the GLM analysis.

claim: A significant proportion of units (~41% of cue-modulated units) discriminated between the arms of the apparatus (location coding), accounting for ~4% of firing rate variance.
source: or the arms of the apparatus (location coding: ~41% of cue-modulated units, accounting for ~4% of firing rate variance) throughout the entire window surrounding cue-onset.
evidence: This is a result from the GLM analysis.

claim: A substantial proportion of units (~20% of cue-modulated units) discriminated between the common portion of reward-available and reward-unavailable trials (outcome coding), accounting for ~4% of firing rate variance.
source: Additionally, a substantial proportion of units discriminating between the common portion of reward-available and reward-unavailable trials (outcome coding: ~20% of cue-modulated units, accounting for ~4% of firing rate variance) was not observed until after the onset of the cue (z-score > 1.96 when comparing observed proportion of units to a shuffled distribution obtained when shuffling the firing rates of each unit across trials before running the GLM).
evidence: This is a result from the GLM analysis.

claim: The observed coding was not due to potential confounds from other task variables, such as behavioural response at the choice point, variability in response vigor, drift due to the passage of time, and the pseudorandom nature of cue presentation.
source: Furthermore, our variable selection method ensured that the observed coding was not due to potential confounds from other task variables, such as behavioural response at the choice point (approach behaviour; left vs. right), variability in response vigor (trial length; see McGinty et al., 2013), drift due to the passage of time (trial number), and the pseudorandom nature of cue presentation (trial history).
evidence: This describes the control for confounds in the analysis.

claim: A similar proportion of outcome coding units (~26% of cue-modulated units) was found when running the cue-onset GLM using only approach trials.
source: In addition to accounting for firing rate variance explained due to whether the rat turned left or right, we ran our cue-onset GLM using only approach trials, and found a similar proportion of outcome coding units (34 units; ~26% of cue-modulated units), providing further support that these units were coding the expected outcome of the cue.
evidence: This is a result from a control analysis.

claim: The NAc encodes features of outcome-predictive cues in addition to expected outcome.
source: Taken together, these results from the GLMs suggest that the NAc encodes features of outcome-predictive cues in addition to expected outcome.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the GLM analysis.

claim: A linear discriminant analysis (LDA) classifier with 10-fold cross-validation could correctly predict a trial above chance levels for the identity and location of a cue across all time points surrounding cue-onset.
source: A linear discriminant analysis (LDA) classifier with 10-fold cross-validation could correctly predict a trial above chance levels for the identity and location of a cue across all time points surrounding cue-onset (z-score > 1.96 when comparing classification accuracy of data versus a shuffled distribution)
evidence: This is a result from the LDA classification analysis.

claim: The ability to predict whether a trial was reward-available or reward-unavailable (outcome coding) was not significantly higher than the shuffled distribution for the time point containing 500 ms of pre-cue firing rate, and increased gradually as a trial progressed.
source: whereas the ability to predict whether a trial was reward-available or reward-unavailable (outcome coding) was not significantly higher than the shuffled distribution for the time point containing 500 ms of pre-cue firing rate, and increased gradually as a trial progressed, providing evidence that cue information is also present at the pseudoensemble level.
evidence: This is a result from the LDA classification analysis.

claim: Cue information is present at the pseudoensemble level.
source: whereas the ability to predict whether a trial was reward-available or reward-unavailable (outcome coding) was not significantly higher than the shuffled distribution for the time point containing 500 ms of pre-cue firing rate, and increased gradually as a trial progressed, providing evidence that cue information is also present at the pseudoensemble level.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the LDA classification analysis.

claim: Identity was coded independently from outcome (mean r = .01, z-score = 0.81).
source: This revealed that identity was coded independently from outcome (mean r = .01, z-score = 0.81)
evidence: This is a result from the correlation analysis of recoded beta coefficients.

claim: Identity was coded by a joint population with location (mean r = .10, z-score = 6.61).
source: and by a joint population with location (mean r = .10, z-score = 6.61)
evidence: This is a result from the correlation analysis of recoded beta coefficients.

claim: Location and outcome were coded by a joint population of units (mean r = .12, z-score = 8.07).
source: while location and outcome were coded by a joint population of units (mean r = .12, z-score = 8.07).
evidence: This is a result from the correlation analysis of recoded beta coefficients.

claim: Various cue features are represented in the NAc at both the single-unit and pseudoensemble level.
source: Together, these findings show that various cue features are represented in the NAc at both the single-unit and pseudoensemble level, with location being coded by joint populations with identity and outcome, but that identity is coded independently from outcome.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analyses.

claim: Location is coded by joint populations with identity and outcome.
source: Together, these findings show that various cue features are represented in the NAc at both the single-unit and pseudoensemble level, with location being coded by joint populations with identity and outcome, but that identity is coded independently from outcome.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analyses.

claim: Identity is coded independently from outcome.
source: Together, these findings show that various cue features are represented in the NAc at both the single-unit and pseudoensemble level, with location being coded by joint populations with identity and outcome, but that identity is coded independently from outcome.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the analyses.

claim: A nearly uniform distribution of firing fields in task space was found that was not limited to alignment to the cue.
source: We did this separately for both the light and sound blocks, and found a nearly uniform distribution of firing fields in task space that was not limited to alignment to the cue (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a result from the population activity analysis, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: While there was some preservation of order, the overall firing was qualitatively different across the two blocks, implying that population activity distinguishes between light and sound blocks.
source: This revealed that while there was some preservation of order, the overall firing was qualitatively different across the two blocks, implying that population activity distinguishes between light and sound blocks.
evidence: This is a result from the population activity analysis.

claim: Within-block correlations were higher and more similar than across-block correlations, suggesting that activity in the NAc discriminates across light and sound blocks.
source: A linear mixed effects model revealed that within-block correlations (e.g. one half of light trials vs other half of light trials) were higher and more similar than across-block correlations (e.g. half of light trials vs half of sound trials) suggesting that activity in the NAc discriminates across light and sound blocks (mean within-block correlation = 0.38; mean across-block correlation = 0.34; p < .001).
evidence: This is a result from the correlation analysis of firing rates.

claim: NAc coding of task space was not confined to salient events such as cue-onset, but was approximately uniformly distributed throughout the task.
source: Together, these results illustrate that NAc coding of task space was not confined to salient events such as cue-onset, but was approximately uniformly distributed throughout the task.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the population activity analysis.

claim: A variety of units discriminated firing according to cue identity (~20% of cue-modulated units) during the post-approach period.
source: This analysis showed that a variety of units discriminated firing according to cue identity (~20% of cue-modulated units) location (~25% of cue-modulated units), and outcome (~25% of cue-modulated units), but not other task parameters, showing that NAc activity discriminates various cue conditions well into a trial.
evidence: This is a result from the GLM analysis aligned to nosepoke and outcome.

claim: A variety of units discriminated firing according to cue location (~25% of cue-modulated units) during the post-approach period.
source: This analysis showed that a variety of units discriminated firing according to cue identity (~20% of cue-modulated units) location (~25% of cue-modulated units), and outcome (~25% of cue-modulated units), but not other task parameters, showing that NAc activity discriminates various cue conditions well into a trial.
evidence: This is a result from the GLM analysis aligned to nosepoke and outcome.

claim: A variety of units discriminated firing according to cue outcome (~25% of cue-modulated units) during the post-approach period.
source: This analysis showed that a variety of units discriminated firing according to cue identity (~20% of cue-modulated units) location (~25% of cue-modulated units), and outcome (~25% of cue-modulated units), but not other task parameters, showing that NAc activity discriminates various cue conditions well into a trial.
evidence: This is a result from the GLM analysis aligned to nosepoke and outcome.

claim: NAc activity discriminates various cue conditions well into a trial.
source: This analysis showed that a variety of units discriminated firing according to cue identity (~20% of cue-modulated units) location (~25% of cue-modulated units), and outcome (~25% of cue-modulated units), but not other task parameters, showing that NAc activity discriminates various cue conditions well into a trial.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the GLM analysis aligned to nosepoke and outcome.

claim: Identity coding was accomplished by a joint population across all three task events (cue-onset, nosepoke, and outcome).
source: This revealed that identity coding was accomplished by a joint population across all three task events (cue-onset and nosepoke: mean r = .05, z-score = 3.47; cue-onset and outcome: mean r = .08, z-score = 5.55; nosepoke and outcome: mean r = .15, z-score = 10.91).
evidence: This is a result from the correlation analysis of recoded beta coefficients across time.

claim: Outcome coding at cue-onset was separate from coding at nosepoke (mean r = −0.04, z-score = −3.10).
source: However, outcome coding at cue-onset was separate from coding at nosepoke (mean r = −0.04, z-score = −3.10)
evidence: This is a result from the correlation analysis of recoded beta coefficients across time.

claim: Joint coding of outcome was observed between nosepoke and outcome (mean r = .15, z-score = 9.74).
source: while joint coding was observed between nosepoke and outcome (mean r = .15, z-score = 9.74).
evidence: This is a result from the correlation analysis of recoded beta coefficients across time.

claim: The NAc maintains representations of cue identity and location by a joint overlapping population throughout a trial.
source: Together, these findings show that the NAc maintains representations of cue identity and location by a joint overlapping population throughout a trial, while separate populations of units encode cue outcome before and after a behavioural decision has been made.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the correlation analysis across time.

claim: Separate populations of units encode cue outcome before and after a behavioural decision has been made.
source: Together, these findings show that the NAc maintains representations of cue identity and location by a joint overlapping population throughout a trial, while separate populations of units encode cue outcome before and after a behavioural decision has been made.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the correlation analysis across time.

claim: Joint coding of cue features was observed at the time of nosepoke (cue identity and location: mean r = .12, z-score = 8.26; cue identity and outcome: mean r = .05, z-score = 3.65; cue location and outcome: mean r = .10, z-score = 6.60).
source: This revealed joint coding of cue features at the time of nosepoke (cue identity and location: mean r = .12, z-score = 8.26; cue identity and outcome: mean r = .05, z-score = 3.65; cue location and outcome: mean r = .10, z-score = 6.60)
evidence: This is a result from the correlation analysis of recoded beta coefficients at nosepoke.

claim: At outcome, identity was coded by a joint population with both location (mean r = .09, z-score = 5.58), and outcome (mean r = .04, z-score = 2.93).
source: while at outcome, identity was coded by a joint population with both location (mean r = .09, z-score = 5.58), and outcome (mean r = .04, z-score = 2.93)
evidence: This is a result from the correlation analysis of recoded beta coefficients at outcome.

claim: At outcome, location and outcome were coded by an independent population of units (mean r = .00, z-score = 0.28).
source: and location and outcome were coded by an independent population of units (mean r = .00, z-score = 0.28).
evidence: This is a result from the correlation analysis of recoded beta coefficients at outcome.

claim: A clustering of responses around outcome receipt was revealed for all cue conditions where the rat would have received reward.
source: This revealed a clustering of responses around outcome receipt for all cue conditions where the rat would have received reward, in addition to the same pattern of higher within- vs across-block correlations for cue identity (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,C; mean within-block correlation = 0.55; mean across-block correlation = 0.48; p < .001), cue location (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B,E; mean within-block correlation = 0.47; mean across-block correlation = 0.41; p < .001), and cue outcome (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C,F; mean within-block correlation = 0.51; mean across-block correlation = 0.41; p < .001), further reinforcing that NAc activity distinguishes all task phases.
evidence: This is a result from the population activity analysis aligned to nosepoke, shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: NAc activity distinguishes all task phases.
source: This revealed a clustering of responses around outcome receipt for all cue conditions where the rat would have received reward, in addition to the same pattern of higher within- vs across-block correlations for cue identity (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A,C; mean within-block correlation = 0.55; mean across-block correlation = 0.48; p < .001), cue location (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B,E; mean within-block correlation = 0.47; mean across-block correlation = 0.41; p < .001), and cue outcome (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C,F; mean within-block correlation = 0.51; mean across-block correlation = 0.41; p < .001), further reinforcing that NAc activity distinguishes all task phases.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the population activity analysis.

claim: The main result of the present study is that NAc units encode not only the expected outcome of outcome-predictive cues, but also the identity of such cues.
source: The main result of the present study is that NAc units encode not only the expected outcome of outcome-predictive cues, but also the identity of such cues (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the Discussion.

claim: The population of units that coded for cue identity was statistically independent from the population coding for expected outcome at cue-onset.
source: The population of units that coded for cue identity was statistically independent from the population coding for expected outcome at cue-onset (i.e. overlap as expected from chance)
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the correlation analysis.

claim: A joint overlapping population coded for identity and outcome at both nosepoke and outcome receipt.
source: while a joint overlapping population coded for identity and outcome at both nosepoke and outcome receipt (i.e. overlap greater than that expected from chance, Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the correlation analysis.

claim: Cue identity information was maintained on approach trials by a similar population of units both during a delay period where the rat held a nosepoke until the outcome was received, and immediately after outcome receipt.
source: Importantly, this identity coding was maintained on approach trials by a similar population of units both during a delay period where the rat held a nosepoke until the outcome was received, and immediately after outcome receipt (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the correlation analysis across time.

claim: Cue identity information was present at the population level, as indicated by high classification performance based on pseudoensembles.
source: Cue identity information was also present at the population level, as indicated by high classification performance based on pseudoensembles.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the LDA classification analysis.

claim: NAc unit activity profiles were not limited to salient task events such as the cue, nosepoke and outcome, but were distributed more uniformly throughout the task.
source: More generally, NAc unit activity profiles were not limited to salient task events such as the cue, nosepoke and outcome, but were distributed more uniformly throughout the task.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the population activity analysis.

claim: The temporally distributed activity differed systematically between cue identities, expected outcomes and locations.
source: This temporally distributed activity differed systematically between cue identities, expected outcomes and locations.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the Discussion based on the population activity analysis.

claim: The finding that NAc units can discriminate between different outcome-predictive stimuli with similar motivational significance expands upon an extensive rodent literature examining NAc correlates of conditioned stimuli.
source: Our finding that NAc units can discriminate between different outcome-predictive stimuli with similar motivational significance (i.e. encode cue identity) expands upon an extensive rodent literature examining NAc correlates of conditioned stimuli (Ambroggi et al., 2008; Atallah et al., 2014; Bissonette et al., 2013; Cooch et al., 2015; Day et al., 2006; Dejean et al., 2017; Goldstein et al., 2012; Ishikawa et al., 2008; Lansink et al., 2012; McGinty et al., 2013; Nicola et al., 2004; Roesch et al., 2009; Roitman et al., 2005; Saddoris et al., 2011; Setlow et al., 2003; Sugam et al., 2014; West and Carelli, 2016; Yun et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the findings in relation to previous literature.

claim: Cooch et al. (2015) found a subset of NAc units that modulated their firing for an odor when it predicted distinct but equally valued rewards.
source: Perhaps the most comparable work in rodents comes from a study that found a subset of NAc units that modulated their firing for an odor when it predicted distinct but equally valued rewards (Cooch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a citation to previous work.

claim: The present study is complementary to outcome identity coding, in showing that NAc units encode cue identity in addition to the reward it predicts.
source: The present study is complementary to such outcome identity coding, in showing that NAc units encode cue identity in addition to the reward it predicts (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a claim about the relationship of the present study to previous work.

claim: Setlow et al. (2003) paired two distinct odor cues with appetitive and aversive odor cues respectively in a Go/NoGo task, such that cue identity and cue outcome were linked.
source: Setlow et al. (2003) paired two distinct odor cues with appetitive and aversive odor cues respectively in a Go/NoGo task, such that cue identity and cue outcome were linked.
evidence: This is a citation to previous work.

claim: The present study is distinct in asking how different cues encoding the same anticipated outcome are encoded.
source: Thus, our study is distinct in asking how different cues encoding the same anticipated outcome are encoded.
evidence: This is a claim about the distinctiveness of the present study.

claim: The NAc dissociates cue identity representations at multiple levels of analysis even when the motivational significance of these stimuli is identical.
source: Our results suggest that the NAc dissociates cue identity representations at multiple levels of analysis (e.g. single-unit and population) even when the motivational significance of these stimuli is identical.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study.

claim: fMRI studies have found support for NAc representations of offer value, a domain-general common currency signal that enables comparison of different attributes.
source: Viewed within the neuroeconomic framework of decision making, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies have found support for NAc representations of offer value, a domain-general common currency signal that enables comparison of different attributes such as reward identity, effort, and temporal proximity (Bartra et al., 2013; Levy and Glimcher, 2012; Peters and Büchel, 2009; Sescousse et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a citation to previous fMRI work.

claim: The study adds to a growing body of electrophysiological research that suggests the view of the NAc as a value centre neglects additional contributions of NAc to learning and decision making such as the offer (cue) identity signal reported here.
source: Our study adds to a growing body of electrophysiological research that suggests the view of the NAc as a value centre, while informative and capturing major aspects of NAc processing, neglects additional contributions of NAc to learning and decision making such as the offer (cue) identity signal reported here.
evidence: This is a claim about the significance of the findings in relation to the neuroeconomic framework.

claim: Units that discriminated between cue identities could instead be encoding time or other slowly-changing quantities because the different cues were separated into different blocks.
source: Because the different cues were separated into different blocks, units that discriminated between cue identities could instead be encoding time or other slowly-changing quantities.
evidence: This is a potential alternative interpretation discussed.

claim: Units that showed a drift in firing between the first and second half within a block were excluded to eliminate the confound of time encoding.
source: We excluded this possible confound by excluding units that showed a drift in firing between the first and second half within a block.
evidence: This describes a control for a potential confound.

claim: Time was included as a nuisance variable in the GLMs to exclude firing rate variance that could be attributed to this confound.
source: Additionally, we included time as a nuisance variable in our GLMs, to exclude firing rate variance in the remaining units that could be attributed to this confound.
evidence: This describes a control for a potential confound.

claim: The temporally evolving firing rate throughout a trial was more strongly correlated within a block than across blocks.
source: Furthermore, we found that the temporally evolving firing rate throughout a trial was more strongly correlated within a block than across blocks.
evidence: This is a result that addresses the potential confound of time encoding.

claim: The possibility remains that instead of, or in addition to, stimulus identity, these units encode a preferred context, or even a macro-scale representation of progress through the session.
source: However, the possibility remains that instead of, or in addition to, stimulus identity, these units encode a preferred context, or even a macro-scale representation of progress through the session.
evidence: This is a discussion of alternative interpretations.

claim: Encoding of the current strategy could be an explanation for the presence of pre-cue identity coding.
source: Indeed, encoding of the current strategy could be an explanation for the presence of pre-cue identity coding (Figure 4A), as well as for the differential distributed coding of task structure across blocks observed in the current study (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Rats were never presented with both sets of cues simultaneously.
source: An overall limitation of the current study is that rats were never presented with both sets of cues simultaneously, and were not required to switch strategies between multiple sets of cues (this was attempted in behavioural pilots, but animals took several days of training to successfully switch strategies).
evidence: This is a limitation of the study discussed.

claim: Recordings were done during performance on the well-learned behaviour, and not during the initial acquisition of the cue-outcome relationships.
source: Additionally, our recordings were done during performance on the well-learned behaviour, and not during the initial acquisition of the cue-outcome relationships when an eligibility trace would be most useful.
evidence: This is a limitation of the study discussed.

claim: It is unknown to what extent the cue identity encoding observed is behaviourally relevant.
source: Thus, it is unknown to what extent the cue identity encoding we observed is behaviourally relevant, although extrapolating data from other work (Sleezer et al., 2016) suggests that cue identity coding would be modulated by relevance.
evidence: This is a discussion of the limitations and implications of the findings.

claim: NAc core lesions have been shown to impair shifting between different behavioural strategies.
source: Furthermore, NAc core lesions have been shown to impair shifting between different behavioural strategies (Floresco et al., 2006)
evidence: This is a citation to previous work.

claim: It is possible that selectively silencing the units that prefer responding for a given modality or rule would impair performance when the animal is required to use that information.
source: and it is possible that selectively silencing the units that prefer responding for a given modality or rule would impair performance when the animal is required to use that information, or artificial enhancement of those units would cause them to use the rule when it is the inappropriate strategy.
evidence: This is a speculative discussion of potential future experiments.

claim: A substantial number of cue-modulated units was differentially active depending on location, consistent with previous reports.
source: First, a substantial number of cue-modulated units was differentially active depending on location, consistent with previous reports (Lavoie and Mizumori, 1994; Mulder et al., 2005; Strait et al., 2016; Wiener et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a finding discussed in relation to previous literature.

claim: In the task, location is explicitly uninformative about reward, yet coding of this uninformative variable persists.
source: However, it is notable that in our task, location is explicitly uninformative about reward, yet coding of this uninformative variable persists.
evidence: This is a discussion of the significance of the location coding finding.

claim: Previous work found location coding in the dorsolateral striatum was present when location was predictive of reward, and absent when it was uninformative.
source: This is unlike previous work of location coding in the dorsolateral striatum, which was present when location was predictive of reward, and absent when it was uninformative (Schmitzer-Torbert and Redish, 2008).
evidence: This is a citation to previous work for comparison.

claim: Persistent coding of location in the NAc is likely attributable to inputs from the hippocampus.
source: Persistent coding of location in the NAc is likely attributable to inputs from the hippocampus (Lansink et al., 2016; Sjulson et al., 2018; Tabuchi et al., 2000; van der Meer and Redish, 2011)
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Speculatively, location coding may map onto a bias in credit assignment, such that motivationally relevant events are likely to be associated with the locations where they occur.
source: speculatively, this coding may map onto a bias in credit assignment, such that motivationally relevant events are likely to be associated with the locations where they occur.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the functional significance of location coding.

claim: NAc units were not only active at salient events such as cue presentation, nosepoking, and feedback about the outcome, but distributed their activity throughout a trial.
source: A second striking feature of NAc activity evident from this task is that NAc units were not only active at salient events such as cue presentation, nosepoking, and feedback about the outcome, but distributed their activity throughout a trial (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding discussed, illustrated in Figure 5.

claim: This observation is consistent with previous work reporting that NAc units can signal progress through a sequence of cues and/or actions.
source: This observation is consistent with previous work reporting that NAc units can signal progress through a sequence of cues and/or actions (Atallah et al., 2014; Berke et al., 2009; Khamassi et al., 2008; Lansink et al., 2012; Mulder et al., 2004; Shidara et al., 1998)
evidence: This is a citation to previous work for comparison.

claim: The observation of distributed NAc activity is reminiscent of similar observations in the ventral pallidum to which the NAc projects.
source: and reminiscent of similar observations in the ventral pallidum (Tingley et al., 2014) to which the NAc projects.
evidence: This is a citation to previous work for comparison.

claim: The specific pattern of NAc units throughout a trial can be modified by task variables such as cue identity.
source: Extending this previous work, we show that the specific pattern of NAc units throughout a trial can be modified by task variables such as cue identity.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings in relation to previous work.

claim: This richer view of NAc activity recalls a dynamical systems perspective, in which different task conditions correspond to different trajectories in a neural state space.
source: This richer view of NAc activity recalls a dynamical systems perspective, in which different task conditions correspond to different trajectories in a neural state space (e.g. Buonomano and Maass, 2009; Shenoy et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by citations.

claim: This view of NAc activity provides a substantially richer picture than that expected from encoding of reward-related variables alone.
source: In any case, this view of NAc activity provides a substantially richer picture than that expected from encoding of reward-related variables alone.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: One possible function of cue identity coding is to support contextual modulation of the motivational relevance of specific cues.
source: One possible function of cue identity coding is to support contextual modulation of the motivational relevance of specific cues.
evidence: This is a speculative discussion of the functional significance of the findings.

claim: A context can be understood as a particular mapping between specific cues and their outcomes.
source: A context can be understood as a particular mapping between specific cues and their outcomes: for instance, in context one cue A but not cue B is rewarded, whereas in context two cue B but not cue A is rewarded.
evidence: This is a definition of context in the discussion.

claim: Successfully implementing contextual mappings requires representation of the cue identities.
source: Successfully implementing such contextual mappings requires representation of the cue identities.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for contextual processing.

claim: Sleezer et al. (2016) recorded NAc responses during the Wisconsin Card Sorting Task and found units that preferred firing to stimuli when a certain rule, or rule category was currently active.
source: Indeed, Sleezer et al. (2016) recorded NAc responses during the Wisconsin Card Sorting Task, a common set-shifting task used in both the laboratory and clinic, and found units that preferred firing to stimuli when a certain rule, or rule category was currently active.
evidence: This is a citation to previous work.

claim: An fMRI study found that bilateral NAc activity reflected value representations for the currently relevant stimulus dimension, and not the irrelevant stimulus dimension during a set-shifting task.
source: Further support for a modulation of NAc responses by strategy comes from an fMRI study that examined blood-oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) levels during a set-shifting task (FitzGerald et al., 2014). In this task, participants learned two sets of stimulus-outcome contingencies, a visual set and an auditory set. During testing they were presented with both simultaneously, and the stimulus dimension that was relevant was periodically shifted between the two. It was found that bilateral NAc activity reflected value representations for the currently relevant stimulus dimension, and not the irrelevant stimulus dimension.
evidence: This is a citation to previous fMRI work.

claim: BOLD activity is thought to reflect the processing of incoming and local information, and not spiking output.
source: Given that BOLD activity is thought to reflect the processing of incoming and local information, and not spiking output (Logothetis et al., 2001)
evidence: This is a citation to previous work about BOLD activity.

claim: It is possible that the relevance-gated value representations observed by FitzGerald et al. (2014) are integrated with the relevant identity coding in the output of the NAc, as observed in the current study.
source: it is possible that the relevance-gated value representations observed by FitzGerald et al. (2014) are integrated with the relevant identity coding in the output of the NAc, as observed in the current study.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation connecting the current findings to previous fMRI work.

claim: A different potential role for cue identity coding is in learning to associate rewards with reward-predictive features of the environment, a process referred to as credit assignment in the reinforcement learning literature.
source: A different potential role for cue identity coding is in learning to associate rewards with reward-predictive features of the environment, a process referred to as credit assignment in the reinforcement learning literature (Sutton and Barto, 1998).
evidence: This is a speculative discussion of the functional significance of the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Maladaptive decision making can result from dysfunctional reward prediction errors (RPEs) and value signals.
source: Maladaptive decision making, as occurs in schizophrenia, addiction, Parkinson's disease and others can result from dysfunctional reward prediction errors (RPEs) and value signals (Frank et al., 2004; Gradin et al., 2011; Maia and Frank, 2011).
evidence: This is a citation to previous work.

claim: This view has been successful in explaining both positive and negative symptoms in schizophrenia, and deficits in learning from feedback in Parkinson's.
source: This view has been successful in explaining both positive and negative symptoms in schizophrenia, and deficits in learning from feedback in Parkinson's (Frank et al., 2004; Gradin et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a citation to previous work.

claim: The effects of RPE and value updating are contingent upon encoding of preceding action and cue features, the eligibility trace.
source: However, the effects of RPE and value updating are contingent upon encoding of preceding action and cue features, the eligibility trace (Lee et al., 2012; Sutton and Barto, 1998).
evidence: This is a citation to reinforcement learning literature.

claim: Value updates can only be performed on aspects of preceding experience that are encoded when the update occurs.
source: Value updates can only be performed on these aspects of preceding experience that are encoded when the update occurs.
evidence: This is a logical inference about credit assignment.

claim: Maladaptive learning and decision making can result from not only aberrant RPEs but also from altered cue feature encoding.
source: Therefore, maladaptive learning and decision making can result from not only aberrant RPEs but also from altered cue feature encoding.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of the findings.

claim: Coding of cue identity and location was found alongside the expected outcome of the cue that could be the outcome of credit assignment computations computed upstream.
source: Although in our current study, the location and identity of the cue did not require any adjustments in the animal's behaviour, we found coding of these features alongside the expected outcome of the cue that could be the outcome of credit assignment computations computed upstream (Akaishi et al., 2016; Asaad et al., 2017; Chau et al., 2015; Noonan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: Identifying neural coding related to an aspect of credit assignment is important as inappropriate credit assignment could be a contributor to conditioned fear overgeneralization seen in disorders with pathological anxiety.
source: Identifying neural coding related to an aspect of credit assignment is important as inappropriate credit assignment could be a contributor to conditioned fear overgeneralization seen in disorders with pathological anxiety such as generalized anxiety disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder (Kaczkurkin et al., 2017; Kaczkurkin and Lissek, 2013; Lissek et al., 2014)
evidence: This is a speculative discussion of the clinical significance of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: Inappropriate credit assignment could be a contributor to delusions observed in disorders such as schizophrenia, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's.
source: and delusions observed in disorders such as schizophrenia, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's (Corlett et al., 2010; Kapur, 2003).
evidence: This is a speculative discussion of the clinical significance of the findings, supported by citations.

claim: The results provide a starting point for studies of the neural basis of credit assignment, and the extent and specific manner in which this process fails in syndromes such as schizophrenia, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and others.
source: Thus, our results provide a starting point for studies of the neural basis of credit assignment, and the extent and specific manner in which this process fails in syndromes such as schizophrenia, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and others.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: A sample size of 4 adult male Long-Evans rats were used as subjects.
source: A sample size of 4 adult male Long-Evans rats (Charles River, Saint Constant, QC) from an a priori determined sample of 5 were used as subjects (one rat was excluded from the data set due to poor cell yield).
evidence: This describes the subjects used in the study.

claim: Rats were individually housed with a 12/12 hr light-dark cycle, and tested during the light cycle.
source: Rats were individually housed with a 12/12 hr light-dark cycle, and tested during the light cycle.
evidence: This describes the housing conditions.

claim: Rats were food restricted to 85–90% of their free feeding weight.
source: Rats were food restricted to 85–90% of their free feeding weight (weight at time of implantation was 440–470 g), and water restricted 4–6 hr before testing.
evidence: This describes the food restriction protocol.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the University of Waterloo Animal Care Committee (protocol# 11–06) and carried out in accordance with Canadian Council for Animal Care (CCAC) guidelines.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the University of Waterloo Animal Care Committee (protocol# 11–06) and carried out in accordance with Canadian Council for Animal Care (CCAC) guidelines.
evidence: This describes the ethical approval for the study.
